catalog_quote: [p. vi] The Be morphemes tend to be monosyllabic, as in the case of many other East and Southeast Asian isolating languages. All the morphological formation of larger meaningful linguistic units of Be takes the form of composites of these syllables, with certain sandhi phenomena of syllable constituents. A Be syllable consists of the initial consonant (hereafter C), the medial vowel (M), the syllabic vowel (V), the ending vowel or consonant (E), and the syllabic musical accent or tone (T) carried by each syllable. Thus the formula for Be syllable is: (C)(M)V(E)T, where constituents given in parentheses are optional. [p. viii] There are in all six syllabic intonations or tones in the Be language. new_statements.quote: [p. vi] A Be syllable consists of the initial consonant (hereafter C), the medial vowel (M), the syllabic vowel (V), the ending vowel or consonant (E), and the syllabic musical accent or tone (T) carried by each syllable. Thus the formula for Be syllable is: (C)(M)V(E)T [...] [p. viii] There are in all six syllabic intonations or tones in the Be language. [...] [p. ix] Tone iii: a middle-level legato tone. The Be tones are neutralized in suffixes and enclitics. The neutralized tones assume the middle-level contour. There is no clear distinction between tone iii and this kind of neutralized tone. In other words, the Be tone-neutralization takes the form of alternation between the original tone and tone iii.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Be (Western Ong-Be, Xinying/Lingao variety) is described purely as a syllable-tone language: every syllable carries one of six tones (four 'legato' tones on open/nasal-final syllables, two 'staccato' tones on stop-final syllables); the author gives no word-stress rule. The only prominence-related facts are tonal: suffixes and enclitics lose their lexical tone and surface with a neutral mid-level tone (= tone iii), and tone i (low-rising with glottal constriction) and tone iv change contour when not phrase-final.
new_statements.exceptions: Tone neutralization is fixed for pure suffixes/enclitics but variable for 'semi-suffixes' (both neutralized and unneutralized forms listed); recent Mandarin loans take a 'non-committal' neutralized mid tone; tone i keeps its citation (low-rising, constricted) shape only in isolation or phrase-finally, otherwise low-falling; tone iv is mid-level in the same non-final position (pp. ix-x).
new_statements.domain_note: Syllable/morpheme-level tone; neutralization defined morphologically (suffixes, enclitics) and tone-i/iv sandhi defined by position in the phonological phrase; citation forms are the 'pronunciation in isolation' shapes.
new_statements.identity_note: Hashimoto 1980 describes the 'Limkow (Lingao) dialect' from one consultant (Lim Bek, resident in Hong Kong); Chen 2018:27 identifies the variety as Xinying 新盈 [xiny1235], a Western Ong-Be dialect under ling1262, so the statement applies to ling1262. Note Glottolog also files Zhou Wen 2019 (Yongxing 永兴) under ling1262, but Yongxing is an Eastern Ong-Be variety [qion1238] in Glottolog's own dialect tree and in Chen 2018. Liang & Zhang 1997 covers Lincheng (Western) and Longtang (Eastern).

sources.note: No word-stress statement. p. vi: syllable = (C)(M)V(E)T, T = 'the syllabic musical accent or tone carried by each syllable'; pp. viii-ix: six tones (4 legato, 2 staccato/checked); p. ix: 'The Be tones are neutralized in suffixes and enclitics. The neutralized tones assume the middle-level contour'; pp. ix-x: tone i (low-rising, glottal constriction) becomes low-falling and tone iv becomes mid-level when not phrase-final and not a suffix/enclitic; recent Mandarin loans take 'non-committal' neutralized mid tone.
